name: PulsePoint AerWork Pro Pulmonary Work Implant
body_location: thoracic — bilateral subpleural diaphragmatic assist nodes with bronchial compliance mesh
description:
The AerWork Pro is a subpleural implant system consisting of two diaphragmatic assist nodes and a fine bronchial compliance mesh that lines the interior of the major airways. The assist nodes — each roughly the size of a grain of rice, embedded just beneath the pleural membrane at the diaphragm's lateral margins — provide rhythmic electromagnetic stimulation that synchronizes with and amplifies the natural contraction of the diaphragm during inhalation, increasing tidal volume by up to 35% and dramatically reducing the effort cost of sustained deep breathing. The bronchial compliance mesh is a passive biocompatible film that slightly increases airway diameter compliance during peak inhalation, reducing resistance and allowing more complete lung fill without increased muscular effort. The combined effect is a meaningful increase in functional oxygen delivery during sustained physical exertion, along with improved CO2 clearance during recovery. The system is powered by a small inductive cell at the lower sternum, charged weekly via a standard LifeWire-compatible body-contact pad.

The AerWork Pro is standard equipment for anyone whose profession demands sustained aerobic output or breath control under load: underwater welders and commercial divers, tunnel construction workers, wildfire suppression crews, high-altitude relay runners, competitive swimmers, and wind instrument performers all rely on it. In GLMZ's industrial zones, where particulate air quality varies significantly and physical labor demands are high, the AerWork Pro is often paired with a SynapTech BreathWatch or AeroSense implant to give workers a complete respiratory monitoring and performance stack. Divers describe the experience as gaining an extra quarter-breath on every cycle — subtle in ordinary life, transformative at depth. Singers and wind players describe better phrase length and more consistent breath support across long performances without the fatigue that once marked the end of a set.
installation_requirements: Thoracic specialist clinic; requires general anesthesia and a four-hour surgical procedure; two-day observation stay recommended; installation by certified thoracic biotech surgeon
maintenance: Biennial thoracic imaging to confirm node placement and mesh integrity; weekly inductive charging via sternum pad; firmware updates for assist-node rhythm calibration pushed annually

side_effects: Mild sensation of 'assisted breathing' during the first month — users describe awareness of the assist rhythm until the nervous system habituates
Occasional brief diaphragmatic flutter during high-stress situations while the system recalibrates to emotional breathing patterns
Slight increase in snoring during the first weeks post-installation as airway compliance adjusts during sleep
Rare: minor pleuritic discomfort at node sites during rapid barometric pressure changes, such as elevator descent in Spire buildings
cultural_context: The AerWork Pro sits at a slightly higher prestige and price point than most mass-market professional implants, and its Licensed status gives it a more medicalized social image. In diving and underwater trades, it is essentially universal — workers without it are considered underprepared. In competitive athletics, it occupies contentious territory: most open amateur circuits allow it freely, but elite competitive swimming and running have 'natural lung' categories alongside augmented divisions, a distinction that generates ongoing debate about what counts as sport versus profession. Among wind instrument musicians, the implant has become quietly common enough that some conservatories have begun updating their breath technique curricula, since the old exercises for building lung capacity are simply less necessary. Tier 1 workers who need it most sometimes struggle with the Licensed requirement and the higher price point, leading to a meaningful gray market in unlicensed installation through thoracic-adjacent street clinics.

Professional wind instrument performers and vocalists
High-altitude relay runners and courier cyclists
story_hooks: A commercial diver has been found dead at depth with her AerWork Pro running at 200% assist — far beyond its rated output — in a configuration that should be firmware-locked. Someone accessed her implant remotely and forced a fatal over-assist that would look on autopsy like a pressure injury. The question is who had the access codes and why.

An unlicensed thoracic installer on the Shelf has been quietly fitting AerWork Pro units sourced from medical surplus — technically legal hardware, illegal installation. Workers who can't afford licensed clinics are going to her. A Lazarus Pharmaceuticals compliance officer is building a case, but the community is protecting her.

A new competitive swimming federation is offering enormous prize purses for an 'unaugmented' invitational — but the verification process relies on an implant scanner that can be fooled by a specific signal spoof. Someone is selling the spoof to augmented swimmers who want to compete in the natural category, and the scandal is about to break publicly.
